sections.section_title: Clinical Approach to Concurrent Behçet’s Disease, Neuro-Behçet’s, and Hyponatremia
sections.description: A practical, bedside-first framework for evaluating patients who present with fever, headache, mucocutaneous lesions, and hyponatremia—recognizing when acute neuro-Behçet’s disease (neuro-BD) and SIADH may coexist and prioritizing immediate safety steps.
key_points: Recognize the syndromic triad: new mucocutaneous lesions (oral and genital ulcers, folliculitis-like rash) + nonspecific CNS symptoms (headache, vertigo, behavioral change) + hyponatremia.
Stabilize first: assess severity of hyponatremia and neurologic symptoms; rule out seizures or severe encephalopathy requiring hypertonic saline.
Rapidly assess volume status; most SIADH is clinically euvolemic; verify by orthostatics, mucous membranes, edema, JVP.
Empirically cover CNS infection when presentation is ambiguous (eg, fever, meningismus, altered mentation) while diagnostic studies are pending.
Consider neuro-BD early when mucocutaneous features coexist with aseptic meningitis-like presentations, even if MRI is initially normal.
Anticipate atypical clues of profound hyponatremia (eg, persistent hiccups) and potential complications (eg, rhabdomyolysis).

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: From Behçet’s Inflammation to Neuroinvolvement and SIADH
sections.description: Mechanistic links among Behçet’s disease immune dysregulation, acute neuro-BD, and dysregulated antidiuretic hormone secretion causing SIADH.
key_points: Behçet’s disease is an autoinflammatory vasculitis with neutrophil hyperactivity and Th1/Th17 skewing; HLA-B51 confers risk but is not diagnostic.

Neuro-BD phenotypes: parenchymal (meningoencephalitis; brainstem/diencephalic predilection) and non-parenchymal (venous sinus thrombosis, intracranial hypertension); early parenchymal disease can have a normal MRI.
CNS inflammation can provoke inappropriate ADH release via cytokine signaling; IL-6 is a candidate mediator implicated in both neuroinflammation and SIADH.
SIADH pathobiology: excess ADH causes free-water retention, concentrated urine, and dilutional hyponatremia despite euvolemia.
Hyponatremia manifestations range from subtle (fatigue, headache, gait disturbance, hiccups) to severe (seizures, coma); profound hyponatremia can precipitate rhabdomyolysis.
Colchicine may attenuate inflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-1β, IL-6) and neutrophil activity, potentially reducing neuroinflammation-driven ADH release, though evidence in neuro-BD is limited.

sections.description: Key alternative diagnoses for febrile meningitic presentations with hyponatremia and for the SIADH phenotype; how to discriminate them from acute neuro-BD and inflammation-driven SIADH.
key_points: Infectious meningoencephalitis: HSV/VZV, enteroviruses, Listeria, TB, cryptococcosis—consider when fever and CSF pleocytosis are present; exclude with CSF PCR/cultures and imaging.
Autoimmune/inflammatory mimics: neurosarcoidosis, CNS vasculitides, AQP4+/MOGAD disorders—guided by systemic signs, MRI patterns, and targeted serologies.
Neoplastic etiologies: primary CNS lymphoma or leptomeningeal carcinomatosis—evaluate with MRI (contrast-enhanced), CSF cytology/flow cytometry.
SIADH etiologies beyond CNS inflammation: pulmonary disease, small cell lung cancer, and medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine).
Endocrine and metabolic mimics of SIADH: hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency must be excluded; correct sodium for hyperglycemia to rule out translocational hyponatremia.
Hyponatremia categories: hypotonic euvolemic (SIADH), hypovolemic (GI losses, diuretics), hypervolemic (heart failure, cirrhosis); pseudohyponatremia with severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia.

sections.description: A stepwise approach integrating BD classification, evaluation of suspected neuro-BD, and a rigorous SIADH assessment, with attention to common pitfalls.
key_points: Classify BD using the International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease (ICBD): oral aphthae (2), genital aphthae (2), ocular (2), skin (1), vascular (1), neurologic (1), pathergy (1); ≥4 points supports BD.

Neuro-BD evaluation: brain MRI with and without contrast (repeat if early study is normal), CSF (opening pressure, cell count with differential, protein, glucose), exclude infection via CSF PCR/cultures.
CSF in acute neuro-BD often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein; oligoclonal bands are typically absent; CSF IL-6 may be elevated (adjunctive, not required).
Ophthalmologic exam for uveitis; document cutaneous and genital lesions; pathergy testing if available; HLA-B51 is supportive but non-diagnostic.

SIADH criteria: hypotonic hyponatremia (low serum osmolality), inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality >100–300 mOsm/kg), urine sodium >30 mmol/L, clinical euvolemia, normal thyroid/adrenal/renal function, and absence of diuretics.
Correct serum sodium for hyperglycemia (~+1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] glucose above normal) to avoid misclassification.
Be judicious with non-specific tests (eg, ACE, sIL-2R) unless supported by clinical context; early MRI can be unrevealing—clinical synthesis remains central.

sections.description: Evidence-based treatment of acute neuro-BD and concurrent SIADH, with practical dosing, sequencing, and safety considerations; positioning of colchicine and immunosuppressants.
key_points: Treat the cause and the consequence: control neuroinflammation (neuro-BD) and correct hyponatremia safely (SIADH).

Acute neuro-BD first-line: high-dose corticosteroids (eg, methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3–5 days) followed by oral taper; add a steroid-sparing agent (eg, azathioprine, methotrexate) for relapsing/refractory disease.
Biologic therapy for refractory/relapsing neuro-BD: TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab); selected cases may benefit from IL-6 blockade, though data are limited.
Avoid cyclosporine in patients with or at risk for neuro-BD due to neurotoxicity risk.

Role of colchicine: effective for mucocutaneous BD; not reliably effective for neuro-BD in systematic reviews, yet may help milder inflammatory phenotypes; can be considered when steroids are undesirable or contraindicated.

SIADH management: fluid restriction (often 500–1000 mL/day), treat underlying inflammation, consider oral salt tablets plus loop diuretics, or urea if needed; vasopressin antagonists (vaptans) are reserved for select cases.

Use hypertonic saline for severe or symptomatic hyponatremia; limit correction to ≤6–8 mmol/L in 24 h (≤18 mmol/L in 48 h) to prevent osmotic demyelination; identify high-risk patients (malnutrition, alcoholism, liver disease, hypokalemia).
Monitor sodium frequently (every 4–6 h initially), track urine output/osmolality, and watch for relapse as inflammation waxes/wanes.
Address comorbidities that worsen outcomes (eg, optimize glycemic control) and provide topical therapies for oral/genital ulcers.

sections.description: Expected clinical course, relapse prevention, and high-yield takeaways that reduce missed diagnoses and iatrogenic harm.
key_points: Acute neuro-BD can be monophasic but carries a risk of relapse and long-term disability with recurrent attacks; early control of inflammation improves outcomes.
Normal early MRI does not exclude neuro-BD; repeat imaging and clinical vigilance are essential.
In BD patients with headache or fever plus hyponatremia, maintain a high index of suspicion for neuro-BD–related SIADH.
Measurement of ADH is not required to diagnose SIADH and may be misleading; rely on standard criteria and exclusion of mimics.
Seemingly unrelated symptoms like persistent hiccups or elevated CK/rhabdomyolysis can be clues to severe hyponatremia.
Prevent iatrogenic harm: avoid indiscriminate testing; correct sodium cautiously; avoid cyclosporine in neuro-BD; tailor immunosuppression intensity to phenotype and relapse risk.
Long-term: monitor for ocular and vascular BD involvement, neurocognitive sequelae, and treatment toxicity; consider prophylactic strategies (eg, steroid-sparing agents) in recurrent neuro-BD.
